blocks.text:
The string is the simplest Redis type and the one you will use most. A string value is a sequence of bytes, nothing more: it can hold text, a number, a serialized Java object, a JSON document, a JPEG. Redis does not care. Almost every other feature in this book (caching, counters, locks, sessions, rate limits) is built on strings, so it pays to know every corner of them.

Strings solve three everyday problems. They let you store a value under a name and read it back in one round trip (a cache entry). They let you change a number atomically on the server without a read-modify-write cycle (a counter). And, with the right `SET` options, they let you make a decision atomically ("create this key only if nobody else has", which is the heart of a lock).

### Reading and writing: SET and GET

The basic pair is `SET key value` and `GET key`. `SET` always overwrites whatever was there, even a value of a different type, and it also discards any TTL (time to live) the key had. `GET` returns the value or `(nil)` when the key does not exist.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> SET user:1:name "Asha"
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> GET user:1:name
"Asha"
127.0.0.1:6379> GET user:2:name
(nil)
127.0.0.1:6379> SET user:1:name "Asha K"
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> STRLEN user:1:name
(integer) 6
blocks.title: Store and read a key

blocks.text: `SET` takes options that turn it into a small toolbox. They are the reason the older commands `SETNX`, `SETEX`, `PSETEX` and `GETSET` are considered legacy: a single `SET` can express all of them.

rows: Set only if the key does not exist
Set only if the key already exists
Return the old value (nil if there was none) instead of OK
Expire at an absolute Unix time (seconds / milliseconds)
Keep the key's current TTL instead of clearing it
blocks.caption: Options of SET (conditions and expiry are two independent groups).

blocks.text: You may combine one condition with one expiry option. Two conditions together (`NX` with `XX`), or two expiry options together, are syntax errors.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> SET session:abc "u42" EX 1800
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL session:abc
(integer) 1800
127.0.0.1:6379> SET session:abc "u42-v2" KEEPTTL
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL session:abc
(integer) 1800
127.0.0.1:6379> SET session:abc "u42-v3"
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL session:abc
(integer) -1
127.0.0.1:6379> SET lock:order:7 "worker-1" NX PX 30000
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> SET lock:order:7 "worker-2" NX PX 30000
(nil)
127.0.0.1:6379> SET missing "x" XX
(nil)
127.0.0.1:6379> SET user:1:name "Asha"
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> SET user:1:name "Asha K" GET
"Asha"
blocks.title: SET with NX, XX, expiry and KEEPTTL

blocks.text: Look at the last three commands. A `NX` that loses the race returns `(nil)`, which is how a lock attempt reports "someone else has it". `XX` on a missing key also returns `(nil)`. And `SET ... GET` returns the previous value while writing the new one, in one atomic step. The third `SET` of `session:abc` shows the trap that `KEEPTTL` exists for: a plain `SET` wipes the TTL (`-1` means "no expiry"), so a session you merely "touch" would live forever.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: A plain `SET` on an existing key removes its TTL. This is the classic way to create an immortal key by accident: you cache something with `EX 600`, later refresh it with a bare `SET`, and it never expires again. Always pass the expiry again, or use `KEEPTTL` when you want to preserve it.

### Reading with side effects: GETEX and GETDEL

Two read commands change the key as they read it, both atomically.

- `GETEX key [EX seconds | PX ms | EXAT ts | PXAT ts | PERSIST]` returns the value and sets or clears its TTL. It is the right tool for a sliding session: read the session and extend its life in one command.
- `GETDEL key` returns the value and deletes the key. It is perfect for one-time tokens such as an e-mail verification code or a "consume once" download link, because two concurrent callers can never both receive the value.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> SET session:abc "u42" EX 60
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> GETEX session:abc EX 1800
"u42"
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL session:abc
(integer) 1800
127.0.0.1:6379> SET otp:asha "493021" EX 300
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> GETDEL otp:asha
"493021"
127.0.0.1:6379> GETDEL otp:asha
(nil)
blocks.title: GETEX and GETDEL

blocks.text:
### Many keys at once: MSET and MGET

`MSET k1 v1 k2 v2 ...` writes many keys and `MGET k1 k2 ...` reads many. Each is one round trip instead of N, which matters because network latency usually dominates the cost of a Redis command (see the chapter on pipelining later in the book). `MSET` is atomic: other clients see all of the writes or none. `MGET` returns `(nil)` in the slot of any missing or non-string key.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> MSET product:1:price 1999 product:2:price 2499 product:3:price 899
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> MGET product:1:price product:3:price product:9:price
1) "1999"
2) "899"
3) (nil)
blocks.title: MSET and MGET

blocks.text:
In a Redis Cluster all keys of one `MSET` or `MGET` must live in the same hash slot, otherwise the command fails with a `CROSSSLOT` error. The cluster chapter explains how hash tags (`{...}` in a key name) solve this.

### Counters: the INCR family

Strings that look like integers can be incremented in place. `INCR` and `DECR` add or subtract one, `INCRBY` and `DECRBY` take an amount, and `INCRBYFLOAT` works with decimals. A key that does not exist is treated as `0`, so the first `INCR` creates it with value `1`. The result is the new value.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> INCR page:home:views
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> INCR page:home:views
(integer) 2
127.0.0.1:6379> INCRBY page:home:views 10
(integer) 12
127.0.0.1:6379> DECR stock:sku-42
(integer) -1
127.0.0.1:6379> INCRBYFLOAT wallet:asha 12.5
"12.5"
127.0.0.1:6379> INCRBYFLOAT wallet:asha -2.25
"10.25"
127.0.0.1:6379> SET greeting "hello"
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> INCR greeting
(error) ERR value is not an integer or out of range
blocks.title: Atomic counters

blocks.text:
The value must be a base-10 signed 64-bit integer. Anything else gives the error you see in the last line. `INCR` past the 64-bit limit also fails instead of wrapping around.

Why is this valuable? Consider the alternative: the application does `GET`, adds one, then `SET`. Two servers doing that at the same moment both read `41` and both write `42`; one increment is lost. `INCR` runs inside the single-threaded command loop, so it is a single indivisible step and no update is ever lost. This is the idea behind page counters, rate limiters, ID generators and stock counters.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Use one `INCR` on a key as a cheap unique ID generator. `INCR seq:order` returns a number nobody else will ever receive from that key. Reserve a block with `INCRBY seq:order 100` if you want to hand out IDs locally without a round trip each time.

### Working with parts of a string

Because strings are byte arrays you can treat them as buffers.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> APPEND log:today "login;"
(integer) 6
127.0.0.1:6379> APPEND log:today "view:42;"
(integer) 14
127.0.0.1:6379> GET log:today
"login;view:42;"
127.0.0.1:6379> GETRANGE log:today 0 4
"login"
127.0.0.1:6379> GETRANGE log:today -3 -1
"42;"
127.0.0.1:6379> SETRANGE log:today 0 "LOGIN"
(integer) 14
127.0.0.1:6379> GET log:today
"LOGIN;view:42;"
blocks.title: APPEND, GETRANGE and SETRANGE

blocks.text:
`GETRANGE key start end` takes inclusive offsets, and negative offsets count from the end (`-1` is the last byte). `SETRANGE` overwrites bytes in place and pads with zero bytes if you write beyond the current end. `APPEND` returns the new length. Appending in a loop is cheap in Redis (amortized), but a key that grows without bound is a memory leak; see the section on big values below.

Redis 7.0 added `LCS`, which computes the longest common subsequence of two string values on the server. It is occasionally useful for diffing two stored versions of a text without downloading them.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> MSET k1 ohmytext k2 mynewtext
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> LCS k1 k2
"mytext"
127.0.0.1:6379> LCS k1 k2 LEN
(integer) 6
blocks.title: LCS: longest common subsequence

blocks.text:
### Compare-and-set and DELEX in Redis 8.4

Locks and optimistic updates need "do this only if the value is still what I think it is". Until recently that required a Lua script or a transaction with `WATCH`. Redis 8.4 added conditions for this directly to `SET` and a new command `DELEX`. The syntax below is quoted from the command reference for 8.4:

blocks.code:
SET key value [NX | XX | IFEQ ifeq-value | IFNE ifne-value |
               IFDEQ ifdeq-digest | IFDNE ifdne-digest]
    [GET] [EX seconds | PX ms | EXAT ts | PXAT ts | KEEPTTL]

DELEX key [IFEQ ifeq-value | IFNE ifne-value |
           IFDEQ ifdeq-digest | IFDNE ifdne-digest]

blocks.text:
- `IFEQ value`: apply only if the current value equals `value`. If the key does not exist, `SET` does not create it.
- `IFNE value`: apply only if the current value differs. If the key does not exist, `SET` creates it.
- `IFDEQ` and `IFDNE` do the same with a digest: a fixed-size XXH3 hash of the value, as a hexadecimal string, which you can obtain with the new `DIGEST` command. Use these when the value is large and you do not want to send it twice.

`DELEX` returns `1` if it deleted the key and `0` if the key was missing or the condition was false. With a condition, the key must hold a string, otherwise it returns an error. The classic use is releasing a lock safely: delete the lock only if it still holds my token.

blocks.code:
# acquire (works on every Redis version)
SET lock:order:7 "worker-1-token" NX PX 30000
# release, Redis 8.4 and later: delete only if I still own it
DELEX lock:order:7 IFEQ "worker-1-token"
# refresh the value only while it is still mine
SET lock:order:7 "worker-1-token" IFEQ "worker-1-token" PX 30000

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: These options exist only in Redis 8.4 and later. On older servers, or on a managed service that has not upgraded, the same release step needs a small Lua script (compare, then `DEL`). The scripting chapter shows it, and the patterns Part uses it for distributed locks. If your code must run on several versions, keep the Lua version.

### What a string really is inside

A string in Redis is stored by an SDS ("simple dynamic string"), a length-prefixed byte buffer. Two consequences follow. It is **binary safe**: it may contain zero bytes and any encoding, because the length is stored explicitly instead of relying on a terminator. And `STRLEN` is O(1). The maximum size of a string value is **512 MB**, but you should never come near that. Large values block the single command thread while they are read, written and sent, and they hurt replication and memory fragmentation. Values of a few kilobytes are comfortable; values over about 100 KB deserve a second look.

Redis picks one of three internal encodings per value, and you can see it with `OBJECT ENCODING`:

rows: Value is an integer that fits in a 64-bit signed long
No separate buffer; the number is stored in the object itself
Object header and buffer live in one allocation: fewer cache misses
Everything longer, or any string that has been modified in place
Header and buffer are separate allocations
blocks.caption: String encodings.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> SET counter 100
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT ENCODING counter
"int"
127.0.0.1:6379> SET name "hello"
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT ENCODING name
"embstr"
127.0.0.1:6379> APPEND name " world"
(integer) 11
127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT ENCODING name
"raw"
127.0.0.1:6379> SET page:html "<html>...a long document of more than forty-four bytes...</html>"
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT ENCODING page:html
"raw"
blocks.title: Observing encodings

blocks.text:
An `embstr` value is read-only: any in-place modification (`APPEND`, `SETRANGE`) converts it to `raw`, as the third line of the session shows. You will rarely tune this, but the sizes explain why millions of tiny string keys cost more memory than you expect: every key has per-entry overhead (the dictionary entry, the key string, the value object) on top of the bytes you store. When you have very many small related values, a hash often costs less; the chapter on hashes explains why.

### A worked example: a fixed-window rate limiter

Counters plus expiry already give you a usable rate limiter. Allow each client IP 5 requests per 60 seconds on the login route. The key encodes the client, the route and the current minute; the first request in a window creates it, and the TTL cleans it up.

blocks.title: Five requests per minute, per IP

blocks.text: The sixth `INCR` returns `6`, which is above the limit of 5, so the application rejects the request (HTTP 429) until the window key expires. The number `29333` is the current Unix time divided by 60, so every minute uses a fresh key. Here is the same idea in Spring code, with `StringRedisTemplate` (the Spring Data Redis Part explains the template in depth):

blocks.text:
What to notice: `increment` maps to `INCR`, so concurrent requests from many gateway instances all see distinct counts. The `expire` call runs only when the count is `1`. There is still the small gap mentioned above: a crash between the two calls would leave a key without TTL. For production, use the Lua version from the rate-limiting chapter. This simple form also allows a burst of up to twice the limit across a window boundary (5 at the end of one minute and 5 at the start of the next), a weakness that the sliding window and token bucket variants remove.

### Strings in practice

#### What to store

A string can hold a plain scalar or a serialized object. For a product cache entry you can store JSON text under `product:42`. This is simple, fast to read in one command, and works with any language. The price is that you replace the whole value to change one field. If you need to read or update single fields, use a hash or the JSON type instead. The Spring Data Redis Part shows how serializers turn a Java object into bytes and back.

#### Typical uses in ShopStream

- **Catalogue cache:** `SET product:42 "{...json...}" EX 600` is written by the cache-aside code.
- **Counters:** `INCR page:home:views` for analytics, `DECR stock:sku-42` for inventory (with the safety checks shown in the Lua chapter).
- **Idempotency keys and locks:** `SET idem:req-9f3 "done" NX EX 86400`. A `(nil)` reply tells the second caller that the request was already seen.
- **Feature flags:** `GET ff:new-checkout` returns `"on"` or `"off"`.
- **Rate limit windows:** `INCR rl:1.2.3.4:/login` followed by `EXPIRE` on the first hit.

#### Pitfalls

- Forgetting the TTL. Every cache or session key should expire; set it in the same command as the value (`SET ...` `EX`) so there is no moment when the key exists without one.
- Doing `INCR` and `EXPIRE` as two separate commands. If the client dies between them, the counter never expires. Wrap both in a transaction or a Lua script, as the rate-limiting chapter shows.
- Treating `INCRBYFLOAT` as exact money arithmetic. It uses floating point. Store money as integer minor units (cents) with `INCRBY`.
- Storing huge blobs. Keep values small; store large files in object storage and keep the URL in Redis.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How do you implement a safe distributed lock with plain Redis strings? Acquire with a single command, `SET lock:key` `<random-token> NX PX <ttl>`. `NX` makes the creation atomic and `PX` guarantees the lock expires even if the holder crashes. Release only if the stored token is still yours, because otherwise you could delete a lock that expired and was re-acquired by someone else. That compare-and-delete must be atomic: a Lua script, or `DELEX key IFEQ token` on Redis 8.4 and later. Mention that a TTL-based lock can still be lost if the holder pauses longer than the TTL, which is why critical work needs fencing tokens.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A string is a binary-safe byte buffer up to 512 MB; keep real values small.
- `SET` with `NX`, `XX`, `GET`, `EX`, `PX`, `KEEPTTL` replaces `SETNX`, `SETEX`, `GETSET`; a bare `SET` clears the TTL.
- `INCR`, `INCRBY`, `DECR` and `INCRBYFLOAT` are atomic, which makes them safe counters under concurrency.
- `GETEX` and `GETDEL` read and change a key in one step; `MSET` and `MGET` save round trips.
- Redis 8.4 adds `IFEQ`, `IFNE`, `IFDEQ`, `IFDNE` to `SET` and the `DELEX` command for compare-and-set and compare-and-delete.
- Encodings are `int`, `embstr` and `raw`; check with `OBJECT ENCODING`.

A Redis list is an ordered sequence of strings, optimized for adding and removing at the two ends. Think of it as a double-ended queue (a "deque") that lives on the server and is shared by every client. Pushing to either end is O(1) no matter how long the list is. That single property makes lists the natural structure for queues, stacks, activity feeds and "latest N items" views.

Lists solve the problem of ordering and hand-off between processes. A web request pushes a job; a worker in another process pops it. The list holds the work in between, and Redis guarantees that each element is popped by exactly one caller.

### The basic commands

Elements are added with `LPUSH` (to the head, the left end) and `RPUSH` (to the tail, the right end). They are removed with `LPOP` and `RPOP`, which also accept a count since Redis 6.2. `LRANGE key start stop` reads a slice using inclusive indexes, where negative indexes count from the tail, so `0 -1` means "everything". A list that becomes empty is deleted automatically, and popping from a missing key returns `(nil)`.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> RPUSH queue:emails a b c
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> LPUSH queue:emails z
(integer) 4
127.0.0.1:6379> LRANGE queue:emails 0 -1
1) "z"
2) "a"
3) "b"
4) "c"
127.0.0.1:6379> LPOP queue:emails
"z"
127.0.0.1:6379> RPOP queue:emails 2
1) "c"
2) "b"
127.0.0.1:6379> LLEN queue:emails
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> LPOP queue:emails
"a"
127.0.0.1:6379> LPOP queue:emails
(nil)
127.0.0.1:6379> EXISTS queue:emails
(integer) 0
blocks.title: Push, pop and range

blocks.text:
Notice the order produced by pushing several values at once. `LPUSH recent a b c` pushes `a`, then `b`, then `c` to the head, so the list reads `c b a`. Each value goes to the head in turn.

Two cheap helpers are worth knowing. `RPUSHX` and `LPUSHX` push only if the list already exists (they return `0` otherwise). `LLEN` returns the length in O(1).

### Reaching into the middle

Lists are not designed for random access, but Redis lets you do it, and you should know what it costs. All of the commands below walk the list from an end, so they are O(N) in the distance travelled.

rows: Element at index i (negative counts from tail)
Replace element at index i; error if out of range
Insert next to the first element equal to pivot
Remove up to count occurrences (count 0 means all; negative counts from the tail)
Find the index (or indexes) of matching elements
Keep only the given range, drop the rest
blocks.caption: Index-based list commands.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> RPUSH l x y z y
(integer) 4
127.0.0.1:6379> LPOS l y
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> LPOS l y RANK 2
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> LPOS l y COUNT 0
1) (integer) 1
2) (integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> LINSERT l BEFORE z mid
(integer) 5
127.0.0.1:6379> LRANGE l 0 -1
1) "x"
2) "y"
3) "mid"
4) "z"
5) "y"
127.0.0.1:6379> LREM l 1 y
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> LRANGE l 0 -1
1) "x"
2) "mid"
3) "z"
4) "y"
127.0.0.1:6379> LSET l 100 a
(error) ERR index out of range
blocks.title: LPOS, LINSERT, LREM

blocks.text: `LPOS` arrived in Redis 6.0.6 and replaces the old pattern of scanning with `LRANGE` on the client. `RANK` selects the n-th match, `COUNT 0` returns all matches, and `MAXLEN` bounds the scan so a huge list cannot hold up the server.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Avoid `LINDEX`, `LSET`, `LINSERT`, `LREM` and `LPOS` on long lists in hot code paths. Redis executes commands one at a time on a single thread. A scan across a list of a million elements blocks every other client for as long as it runs. If you find yourself indexing into a list a lot, you probably want a sorted set (ordered by score) or a hash (addressed by field) instead.

### Pattern 1: a capped "latest N" list

A very common use of lists is a rolling window of recent items: the last 10 searches of a user, the last 100 log lines, the newest 20 notifications. The recipe is `LPUSH` followed by `LTRIM`, which together keep the list bounded.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> LPUSH recent:asha "red shoes"
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> LPUSH recent:asha "usb cable"
(integer) 2
127.0.0.1:6379> LPUSH recent:asha "desk lamp"
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> LPUSH recent:asha "phone case"
(integer) 4
127.0.0.1:6379> LPUSH recent:asha "monitor"
(integer) 5
127.0.0.1:6379> LPUSH recent:asha "keyboard"
(integer) 6
127.0.0.1:6379> LTRIM recent:asha 0 4
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> LRANGE recent:asha 0 -1
1) "keyboard"
2) "monitor"
3) "phone case"
4) "desk lamp"
5) "usb cable"
blocks.title: Recent searches, capped at 5

blocks.text:
If two clients run this at the same moment the list can briefly exceed the cap, but the next `LTRIM` fixes it. To make the pair atomic, send both commands in a `MULTI`/`EXEC` transaction or a pipeline. A newer item that repeats an old one should first be removed with `LREM recent:asha 0 "monitor"` so the list does not hold duplicates.

### Pattern 2: a work queue

The producer pushes to one end, the consumer pops from the other. Use `LPUSH` + `RPOP` (or `RPUSH` + `LPOP`); the direction does not matter as long as you are consistent.

Polling in a loop wastes CPU and adds latency. The blocking variants wait on the server until data arrives:

- `BLPOP key [key ...] timeout` and `BRPOP` block until one of the lists has an element, or the timeout in seconds passes (`0` means wait forever). They return a two-element array: the key name and the value, so that you know which of several lists woke you.
- `BLMPOP timeout numkeys key [key ...] LEFT|RIGHT [COUNT n]` (Redis 7.0) is the modern general form: it can pop several elements at once from the first non-empty list.
- `LMPOP numkeys key [key ...] LEFT|RIGHT [COUNT n]` is the non-blocking twin.

blocks.code:
# terminal 1: waits, no CPU used, no busy loop
127.0.0.1:6379> BLPOP queue:emails 30
# terminal 2:
127.0.0.1:6380> RPUSH queue:emails "welcome:u42"
(integer) 1
# terminal 1 wakes immediately:
1) "queue:emails"
2) "welcome:u42"
(4.21s)
blocks.title: A blocked consumer and a producer (two terminals)

blocks.text:
Blocking commands block only the calling client, not the server. If several consumers wait on the same list, Redis serves them in the order in which they started waiting, one element each. This is the "competing consumers" model: add workers to add throughput.

#### The weakness: a popped job is gone

`BLPOP` removes the element before your code has processed it. If the worker crashes after the pop, the job is lost. For anything that matters you want a reliable queue, and lists support one with `LMOVE`.

`LMOVE source destination LEFT|RIGHT LEFT|RIGHT` atomically pops from one list and pushes onto another, and returns the element. Move each job from `jobs` to a per-worker `jobs:processing` list, do the work, then remove it from the processing list with `LREM` when finished. If a worker dies, a janitor process can find stale entries in the processing lists and push them back. `BLMOVE` is the blocking version. The older `RPOPLPUSH` and `BRPOPLPUSH` do the same thing with fixed directions and are deprecated.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> RPUSH jobs "email:101" "email:102" "email:103"
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> LMOVE jobs jobs:processing:w1 LEFT RIGHT
"email:101"
127.0.0.1:6379> LRANGE jobs:processing:w1 0 -1
1) "email:101"
# ... the worker sends the e-mail, then acknowledges:
127.0.0.1:6379> LREM jobs:processing:w1 1 "email:101"
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> LRANGE jobs:processing:w1 0 -1
(empty array)
127.0.0.1:6379> LRANGE jobs 0 -1
1) "email:102"
2) "email:103"
blocks.title: Reliable queue with LMOVE

blocks.text:
This pattern gives at-least-once delivery: after a crash the same job may run twice, so job handlers must be idempotent. It has no built-in retry counter, delay, or visibility timeout. When you need those, or several independent consumer groups reading the same data, use a stream instead; the streams chapter and the queues chapter in the Patterns Part compare the options.

### Pattern 3: a stack, and a message inbox

A stack is the same list used LIFO: `LPUSH` and `LPOP` on the same end. "Undo history" and "back button" data fit this. For a per-user inbox that is read often and capped, `LPUSH` to add, `LRANGE inbox:u42 0 19` for the first page, and `LTRIM` to bound it. Beyond a few hundred entries or when you need paging by time, prefer a sorted set whose score is a timestamp.

### How lists are stored

Internally, a list is stored as a **quicklist**: a linked list whose nodes each hold a compact array called a **listpack** (the memory-efficient successor of the ziplist). Small lists in recent versions are kept as a single listpack with no linked-list overhead at all. You can check with `OBJECT ENCODING key`, which returns `listpack` or `quicklist` depending on the version and size. Redis 7.0 reports `quicklist` even for a tiny list, while newer versions can report `listpack` for small ones.

The design is a compromise. A plain linked list wastes memory on a pointer pair per element; a plain array makes pushes at the front expensive. A linked list of small arrays gives O(1) pushes at both ends with low overhead per element.

rows: Maximum size of one node. A negative value is a byte limit: -2 means 8 KB per node (-1 is 4 KB, up to -5 for 64 KB). A positive value limits the number of entries
Number of nodes at each end left uncompressed. 0 disables compression; 1 keeps the head and tail nodes plain and compresses the middle
blocks.caption: List configuration directives.

blocks.text:
Compression pays off only for very long lists whose middle is rarely touched (because the ends are what you read). For a typical queue it is better left off.

### Big-list gotchas

- **Unbounded growth.** A queue whose consumers are slower than its producers grows until memory runs out. Cap lists with `LTRIM` where the content is disposable, and alert on `LLEN` for queues.
- `LRANGE 0 -1` **on a long list.** It copies the whole list into one reply. Page with ranges such as `0 99`, then `100 199`.
- **One giant key.** A list of ten million elements lives in one key, on one shard, and deleting it can stall the server. `UNLINK` frees it in a background thread; `DEL` does it inline. In a cluster, consider splitting a queue across several keys (`queue:emails:{0}`, `queue:emails:{1}`) with a client-side choice.
- **Treating it as a database.** Lists cannot answer "which job has id 7" without a scan. Keep an index (a hash from job id to payload) if you need lookups.
- **Lost jobs on** `BLPOP`**.** Covered above: use `LMOVE`, or a stream with acknowledgements.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How would you build a reliable task queue on Redis lists, and where does it fall short? Use `LMOVE` (or `BLMOVE`) to atomically move each job from the pending list to a per-worker processing list, delete it with `LREM` after success, and run a reaper that requeues entries stuck in processing too long. That gives at-least-once delivery, so handlers must be idempotent. It falls short on retries with backoff, delayed jobs, per-job visibility timeouts, dead-letter handling and multiple independent consumers. Streams with consumer groups or a sorted-set delay queue handle those better.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: In ShopStream, the notification-service keeps `recent:{userId}` as a capped list of the last 20 product views for the "recently viewed" strip: `LPUSH`, `LREM` of a duplicate, `LTRIM 0 19`, all in one pipeline. Order events themselves go to a stream, not a list, because several services must read them independently and acknowledge them.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Lists are deques: O(1) push and pop at both ends, O(N) access in the middle.
- `LPUSH` + `LTRIM` gives a capped "latest N" list; `LPUSH` + `BRPOP` gives a simple blocking queue.
- `LMOVE`/`BLMOVE` plus a processing list gives an at-least-once queue; streams are better when you need more.
- `LMPOP` and `BLMPOP` (7.0) pop several elements from the first non-empty of many lists.
- Storage is a quicklist of listpacks; tune `list-max-listpack-size` rarely, and never let a list grow without a bound.
- Page large reads and delete big lists with `UNLINK`.

A hash maps field names to values inside a single key, like a small dictionary or a row of a table. Where a string holds one value, a hash holds a record: `product:42` can carry `name`, `price` and `stock` as separate fields, and you can read or change one field without touching the others.

Hashes solve the "object" problem. Storing a product as one JSON string forces you to download, parse, change and re-upload the entire document to adjust one number, and two clients doing that at once overwrite each other. With a hash, `HINCRBY product:42 stock -1` changes exactly one field, atomically, on the server.

### The core commands

`HSET key field value [field value ...]` creates or updates fields and returns how many fields were newly created. (The old `HMSET` does the same job and only differs in returning `OK`; it is deprecated, use `HSET`.) `HGET` reads one field, `HMGET` reads several, `HGETALL` reads everything as a flat list of alternating field and value.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> HSET product:42 name "USB-C Cable" price 799 stock 120
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> HGET product:42 name
"USB-C Cable"
127.0.0.1:6379> HMGET product:42 name price color
1) "USB-C Cable"
2) "799"
3) (nil)
127.0.0.1:6379> HGETALL product:42
1) "name"
2) "USB-C Cable"
3) "price"
4) "799"
5) "stock"
6) "120"
127.0.0.1:6379> HINCRBY product:42 stock -1
(integer) 119
127.0.0.1:6379> HINCRBYFLOAT product:42 price 0.5
"799.5"
127.0.0.1:6379> HSETNX product:42 name "other"
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> HEXISTS product:42 color
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> HLEN product:42
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> HDEL product:42 price color
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> HKEYS product:42
1) "name"
2) "stock"
blocks.title: A product as a hash

blocks.text: A few details worth remembering. Field values are strings (like everything in Redis), so `price 799` is stored as the text `799`; `HINCRBY` parses it as an integer when you ask. `HSETNX` sets a field only if it does not exist, a handy "initialize once". `HSTRLEN` gives the length of a field's value. `HRANDFIELD` (6.2) returns random fields, optionally with values. Prices in cents as integers keep arithmetic exact.

rows: Write or read one or more fields
Atomic numeric update of a field
Delete fields; the key disappears when the last field goes
Iterate fields in small batches with a cursor
blocks.caption: Hash commands and their cost.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: `HGETALL` on a hash with hundreds of thousands of fields blocks the server. It builds one huge reply on the single command thread. For big hashes read the fields you need with `HMGET`, or walk the hash incrementally with `HSCAN key` `cursor [MATCH pattern] [COUNT n]`. The scan commands are covered in their own chapter.

### Field expiration (Redis 7.4 and later)

A key can expire, but historically a field could not. If you wanted per-field lifetimes (the items of a shopping cart, the temporary flags of a session) you had to split data across many keys. Redis 7.4 added **hash field expiration**, and Redis 8.0 added commands that combine reading or writing with an expiry.

rows: Set a relative TTL (seconds) on fields. HPEXPIRE is the millisecond form; HEXPIREAT and HPEXPIREAT take an absolute Unix time
Remaining TTL per field, in seconds / milliseconds. -1 means the field has no TTL, -2 means the field (or key) does not exist
The absolute expiry time per field
Read fields and set or clear their TTL in one step (8.0)
Write fields with a TTL; FNX only if none exist, FXX only if all exist (8.0)
blocks.caption: Hash field expiration commands.

blocks.text: All of these take the form `FIELDS numfields field [field ...]`: you state how many fields follow, then list them. Commands that set a TTL return one integer per field: `1` the TTL was set, `0` a condition (`NX`, `XX`, `GT`, `LT`) was not met, `-2` no such field, `2` the field was deleted because the TTL was zero or already in the past.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> HSET cart:u42 sku-1 2 sku-2 1 sku-3 5
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> HEXPIRE cart:u42 3600 FIELDS 2 sku-1 sku-9
1) (integer) 1
2) (integer) -2
127.0.0.1:6379> HTTL cart:u42 FIELDS 3 sku-1 sku-2 sku-9
1) (integer) 3600
2) (integer) -1
3) (integer) -2
127.0.0.1:6379> HGETEX cart:u42 EX 7200 FIELDS 1 sku-1
1) "2"
127.0.0.1:6379> HSETEX cart:u42 FXX EX 600 FIELDS 1 sku-2 3
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> HGETDEL cart:u42 FIELDS 1 sku-3
1) "5"
blocks.title: Field TTLs on a cart (Redis 7.4 or later)

blocks.text: When the last field of a hash expires or is deleted, the key itself disappears. Expired fields are removed lazily when touched and by a background process, exactly as keys are (see the chapter on expiration); they are never returned by reads once their time has passed. Expiry of fields is also replicated and persisted like key expiry.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Field expiry does not exist before Redis 7.4. Many managed services lag behind the open source release. If your code must run against an older server, keep the per-field time in the hash as a normal field (an expiry timestamp) and filter on read, or use one key per item.

### A worked example: a session store

A web session is a bundle of small attributes (user ID, locale, CSRF token, last seen) that is read on every request and must disappear after inactivity. A hash with a key TTL fits exactly: one key per session, fields for attributes, the whole thing expiring together.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> HSET session:9f2c userId 42 locale en-IN csrf a81f
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> EXPIRE session:9f2c 1800
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> HGET session:9f2c userId
"42"
127.0.0.1:6379> HSET session:9f2c lastSeen 1760000100
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> EXPIRE session:9f2c 1800
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL session:9f2c
(integer) 1800
127.0.0.1:6379> HGETALL session:9f2c
1) "userId"
2) "42"
3) "locale"
4) "en-IN"
5) "csrf"
6) "a81f"
7) "lastSeen"
8) "1760000100"
blocks.title: Session hash with a sliding TTL

blocks.text:
Each request reads the fields it needs and pushes the expiry forward with `EXPIRE` (a pipeline sends the two commands in one round trip). Only the changed field is written, so concurrent requests from the same browser do not overwrite each other's attributes. When the user is inactive for 30 minutes the key vanishes by itself. Spring Session uses a hash per session in exactly this way, as described in the Spring Part.

### Objects: hash or JSON string?

Both work; they have different strengths.

rows: Not supported; flatten to field names
blocks.caption: Storing an object as a hash or as one serialized string.

blocks.text:
Rule of thumb: use a hash for flat records that you update by field (product stock, user profile, cart lines, session attributes). Use a string holding JSON for a read-mostly document that you always load whole (a cached API response). If you need nested documents with partial updates and indexing, the JSON data type of Redis 8 (covered later in this Part) is designed for that.

### Memory: listpack to hashtable

A small hash is stored as a **listpack**, a single compact array of field and value bytes, with no pointers or per-entry allocations. Lookup in a listpack is a linear scan, which is fast for a handful of entries because they sit together in cache. When the hash exceeds `hash-max-listpack-entries` (default 512 in Redis 7.0 and later) or any field or value is longer than `hash-max-listpack-value` bytes (default 64), Redis converts it to a real **hashtable**, which has O(1) lookup but more memory per field. The conversion happens automatically and is one-way for a given hash (a hash does not shrink back when it loses fields in the usual case).

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> HSET product:42 name "USB-C Cable" price 799
(integer) 2
127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT ENCODING product:42
"listpack"
127.0.0.1:6379> HSET product:42 desc \
  "Braided nylon cable, 2 m, 100 W power delivery, data up to 480 Mbps"
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT ENCODING product:42
"hashtable"
blocks.title: Seeing the encoding

blocks.text: This is why Redis documentation recommends hashes for many small objects: a million users as a million `user:ID` hashes of five fields costs far less than five million separate string keys, because each Redis key carries fixed bookkeeping overhead. A hash that sits just above the thresholds loses that advantage, so keep fields short where you can, and measure with `MEMORY USAGE key`. Release 8.6 further reduces the memory of hashtable-encoded hashes, but the guidance stays the same: small flat hashes are the cheapest representation.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Do not put a million fields in one hash just to save memory. A single huge hash is one key on one shard, it can only expire as a whole key (unless you use field TTLs), and commands like `HGETALL` and `DEL` become latency spikes. Shard by a natural boundary (per user, per product) and keep each hash small to medium.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why store a user profile as a hash instead of JSON in a string? A hash lets you read and update individual fields with O(1) commands and atomic numeric updates (`HINCRBY`) without a read-modify-write cycle, avoids lost updates between concurrent writers, and a small hash uses a compact listpack encoding. JSON in a string is better when the object is nested and always read whole. Add that since 7.4 individual fields can even have their own TTL.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A hash is a record under one key: fields are read and written individually, `HINCRBY` is atomic.
- Use `HSET` (not `HMSET`); avoid `HGETALL` on big hashes and use `HSCAN` or `HMGET`.
- Redis 7.4 added field TTLs (`HEXPIRE`, `HTTL`, `HPERSIST`); 8.0 added `HGETEX`, `HSETEX` and `HGETDEL`.
- Small hashes are listpacks; beyond 512 entries or 64-byte values they convert to hashtables.
- Choose hash for flat, field-updated records; JSON string or the JSON type for nested documents.

A set is an unordered collection of unique strings. Adding the same member twice has no effect, checking membership is O(1), and Redis can combine sets on the server with intersection, union and difference. Where a list answers "what is in order", a set answers "is X in this group, and what do these groups have in common".

Sets solve problems of uniqueness and relationships: the tags on a product, the users who liked a post, the IDs of items already shown to a visitor, the set of users currently online.

### Adding, testing, removing

`SADD key member [member ...]` returns how many members were new. `SISMEMBER` tests one member and `SMISMEMBER` (6.2) tests several in one call. `SREM` removes, `SCARD` returns the size, `SMEMBERS` returns everything. Sets have no defined order, so never depend on the order of the replies shown.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> SADD tags:p1 red cotton sale
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> SADD tags:p1 red
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> SISMEMBER tags:p1 sale
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> SMISMEMBER tags:p1 sale blue
1) (integer) 1
2) (integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> SCARD tags:p1
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> SREM tags:p1 cotton
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> SCARD tags:p1
(integer) 2
blocks.title: Tags as sets
Watch out
blocks.text: `SMEMBERS` on a large set is like `HGETALL` on a large hash. It returns every member in a single reply and blocks the server while doing so. For big sets use `SSCAN key cursor [MATCH pattern] [COUNT n]`, which returns a few members per call.

### Combining sets

The set algebra commands are the reason to choose a set. Take two products and their tags:

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> SADD tags:p1 red cotton sale
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> SADD tags:p2 sale new cotton
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> SINTER tags:p1 tags:p2
1) "cotton"
2) "sale"
127.0.0.1:6379> SUNION tags:p1 tags:p2
1) "new"
2) "cotton"
3) "sale"
4) "red"
127.0.0.1:6379> SDIFF tags:p1 tags:p2
1) "red"
127.0.0.1:6379> SINTERCARD 2 tags:p1 tags:p2
(integer) 2
127.0.0.1:6379> SINTERCARD 2 tags:p1 tags:p2 LIMIT 1
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> SINTERSTORE tags:common tags:p1 tags:p2
(integer) 2
127.0.0.1:6379> SCARD tags:common
(integer) 2
blocks.title: Intersection, union, difference

blocks.text:
- `SINTER` returns members present in all the sets; `SUNION` in any; `SDIFF` returns members of the first set that are in none of the others (the order of the arguments matters).
- Each has a `...STORE` form (`SINTERSTORE`, `SUNIONSTORE`, `SDIFFSTORE`) that saves the result into a destination key instead of returning it. Use these for large results and then page through them.
- `SINTERCARD numkeys key [key ...] [LIMIT n]` (7.0) returns only the size of the intersection, and with `LIMIT` it stops counting early. It answers "how many common tags" without building the result.
- `SMOVE source destination member` moves a member atomically.

The cost of an intersection is bounded by the smallest set times the number of sets, which is why intersections of a small set with large ones are cheap. A union or difference is proportional to the total number of elements. In a Redis Cluster all the keys of one of these commands must hash to the same slot.

### Random members

`SRANDMEMBER key [count]` returns random members without removing them. A negative count allows repeats. `SPOP` `key [count]` removes and returns random members. Together they cover lotteries, random sampling and "pick any available worker".

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> SADD raffle:2026 u1 u2 u3 u4 u5
(integer) 5
127.0.0.1:6379> SCARD raffle:2026
(integer) 5
127.0.0.1:6379> SPOP raffle:2026
"u3"
127.0.0.1:6379> SCARD raffle:2026
(integer) 4
blocks.title: SRANDMEMBER and SPOP

blocks.text:
The replies of `SPOP` and `SRANDMEMBER` are random, so your session will show different members.

### Storage

Sets have three encodings. A set that contains only integers, and not more than `set-max-intset-entries` (default 512), is an **intset**: a sorted array of integers that uses 2, 4 or 8 bytes per number depending on the largest value. In Redis 7.2 and later, a small set of non-integer members (up to `set-max-listpack-entries`, default 128, each at most `set-max-listpack-value` bytes, default 64) is a **listpack**. Everything else is a **hashtable** with the members as keys. Conversion is automatic, and `OBJECT ENCODING` shows the current one.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> SADD nums 1 2 3
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT ENCODING nums
"intset"
127.0.0.1:6379> SADD nums apple
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> OBJECT ENCODING nums
"listpack"
blocks.title: Set encodings (Redis 7.2 and later)

blocks.text:
Add enough members (or one member longer than 64 bytes) and the encoding becomes `hashtable`. Before Redis 7.2 the second answer would already be `hashtable`.

### Patterns for ShopStream

- **Product tags and filters:** keep `tag:cotton` as a set of product IDs, then `SINTER tag:cotton tag:sale` is the list of cotton products on sale. This inverted index is the basis of many small catalogues.
- **Unique counting for small groups:** `SADD viewers:product:42 u1` and `SCARD`. When the group has millions of members and an estimate is fine, use HyperLogLog instead (its chapter follows in this Part).
- **Recommendations:** "customers who bought this also bought" via `SINTER` of buyers of two products, or `SINTERCARD` to count the overlap.
- **Online users and presence:** `SADD online:users u42` on connect, `SREM` on disconnect. Remember a crash leaves stale members, so pair it with a heartbeat sorted set when accuracy matters.
- **Already seen:** `SADD seen:u42 article-9` returns 0 if the user has seen it before, giving a one-command "is this new" test.
- **Allow and deny lists:** a set of IDs that may (or may not) use a feature.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Sets do not expire per member. A member lives until you `SREM` it or the whole key expires. If you need "members that disappear after N minutes" (online presence, recent activity), use a sorted set with the expiry time as the score and delete the old range with `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE`.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A set holds unique, unordered strings with O(1) add, remove and membership test.
- `SINTER`, `SUNION`, `SDIFF`, `SINTERCARD` and the `STORE` forms combine sets on the server; keep the keys in one slot on a cluster.
- Use `SSCAN`, not `SMEMBERS`, on big sets; `SPOP` and `SRANDMEMBER` give random picks.
- Encodings: intset for small integer sets, listpack for small mixed sets (7.2+), hashtable otherwise.
- Great for tags, uniqueness, relationships and seen-lists; use a sorted set when you need order or per-member expiry.

A sorted set (often written "zset" after the command prefix `Z`) is a set of unique members in which every member carries a numeric **score**, and Redis keeps the members ordered by score at all times. You can add a member, change its score, ask for its rank, and fetch the top ten or the range between two scores, each in O(log N) time. No other structure in Redis, and few in any database, gives you a live ranking this cheaply.

That makes sorted sets the answer to a long list of problems: leaderboards, "most popular", time-ordered feeds, delayed job queues, sliding-window rate limiters, priority queues, and any index where you need "everything between A and B".

### Adding members: ZADD and its flags

`ZADD key [NX|XX] [GT|LT] [CH] [INCR] score member [score member ...]`. A new member is inserted; an existing member has its score updated. By default the reply is the number of **new** members, which is why updating a score returns `0`.

rows: Only add new members; never update existing ones
Only update existing members; never add
Update an existing member only if the new score is greater (still adds new members)
Update an existing member only if the new score is less (still adds new members)
Reply with the number of members changed (added plus updated) instead of added
Add the score to the existing one, like ZINCRBY; one pair only, reply is the new score
blocks.caption: ZADD flags.

blocks.text: `NX` and `XX` exclude each other, and `GT`, `LT` and `NX` cannot be combined with each other. `GT` is the right flag for "keep the best score": a player submits many results and only a higher one counts.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD lb:bestsellers 100 asha 250 ravi 175 mei
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD lb:bestsellers 90 asha
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD lb:bestsellers GT CH 120 asha
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD lb:bestsellers GT CH 80 asha
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD lb:bestsellers NX 500 asha
(integer) 0
127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD lb:bestsellers INCR 25 mei
"200"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZSCORE lb:bestsellers mei
"200"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZMSCORE lb:bestsellers mei nobody
1) "200"
2) (nil)
127.0.0.1:6379> ZCARD lb:bestsellers
(integer) 3
blocks.title: Scores, flags and the best-score rule

blocks.text:
Read the sequence carefully. `ZADD ... 90 asha` changed the score from 100 to 90 and still replied `0`, because no new member was created. The two `GT CH` calls show the flag at work: 120 is greater than 90 so it changed (`1`), 80 is not so nothing changed (`0`). Scores are 64-bit floating point numbers. Integers are exact up to 2^53; beyond that, or with fractions, rounding applies. `+inf` and `-inf` are valid scores.

### Reading ranges: ZRANGE

Since Redis 6.2 one command, `ZRANGE`, does all range queries; the older `ZREVRANGE`, `ZRANGEBYSCORE`, `ZREVRANGEBYSCORE`, `ZRANGEBYLEX` are deprecated spellings of it.

blocks.code: ZRANGE key start stop [BYSCORE | BYLEX] [REV] [LIMIT offset count] [WITHSCORES]

blocks.text:
- Plain `ZRANGE key 0 9` selects by **rank** (position): index 0 is the lowest score. Negative indexes count from the end.
- `REV` reverses the order, so `ZRANGE key 0 9 REV` is the top ten. This is the leaderboard query.
- `BYSCORE` interprets start and stop as scores. A leading `(` makes a bound exclusive, and `-inf`/`+inf` mean unbounded. With `REV` the arguments swap: you give the high bound first.
- `BYLEX` selects by member name when all scores are equal, using `[` for inclusive and `(` for exclusive bounds, and `-`/`+` for the extremes. This gives you prefix search and autocomplete over a lexicographic index.
- `LIMIT offset count` pages the result, and is only allowed with `BYSCORE` or `BYLEX`.
- `WITHSCORES` adds each member's score to the reply.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD lb:bestsellers 120 asha 300 ravi 200 mei
(integer) 3
127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGE lb:bestsellers 0 -1
1) "asha"
2) "mei"
3) "ravi"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGE lb:bestsellers 0 -1 WITHSCORES
1) "asha"
2) "120"
3) "mei"
4) "200"
5) "ravi"
6) "300"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGE lb:bestsellers 0 1 REV WITHSCORES
1) "ravi"
2) "300"
3) "mei"
4) "200"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGE lb:bestsellers 150 +inf BYSCORE
1) "mei"
2) "ravi"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGE lb:bestsellers (150 +inf BYSCORE LIMIT 0 1
1) "mei"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGE lb:bestsellers +inf -inf BYSCORE REV LIMIT 0 2 WITHSCORES
1) "ravi"
2) "300"
3) "mei"
4) "200"
127.0.0.1:6379> ZCOUNT lb:bestsellers 100 250
(integer) 2
127.0.0.1:6379> ZADD names 0 alice 0 bob 0 carol 0 dave
(integer) 4
127.0.0.1:6379> ZRANGE names [b (d BYLEX
1) "bob"
2) "carol"
blocks.title: Rank, score and lexicographic ranges

blocks.text:
### Rank, increments and popping

`ZRANK key member` is the 0-based position from the lowest score and `ZREVRANK` from the highest; both are O(log N). Since 7.2 either accepts `WITHSCORE` to also return the score in one call. A missing member gives `(nil)`. `ZINCRBY key` `amount member` is the atomic counter of sorted sets: it creates the member if needed and returns the new score.

`ZPOPMIN` and `ZPOPMAX` remove and return the lowest or highest members (with an optional count), and their blocking forms `BZPOPMIN` and `BZPOPMAX` wait for data, which makes a sorted set a priority queue. `ZMPOP` and `BZMPOP` (7.0) do the same across several keys. `ZREM` removes by member, and `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE`, `ZREMRANGEBYRANK` remove whole ranges.

blocks.text:
### Ties and ordering

When two members have the same score, Redis orders them lexicographically by member (byte comparison). That is deterministic, which is what you want. It is also why the `BYLEX` index works: give every member score 0 and the order is purely alphabetical.

For a leaderboard where ties should be broken by who reached the score first, encode the time into the score itself. One way: keep the real score as a whole number and add a small fraction that shrinks as time passes, for example `score + (1 - timestampMillis / 10^14)`. An earlier timestamp gives a larger fraction, so the earlier player ranks higher among equals. Check that the combined number stays exactly representable as a double (about 15 to 16 significant digits) before adopting any such scheme, or keep the tie-break data in a separate hash.

### Set algebra on sorted sets

Sorted sets can be combined like sets, with a rule for merging the scores of members that appear in several inputs.

- `ZUNIONSTORE dest numkeys key [key ...] [WEIGHTS w ...] [AGGREGATE SUM|MIN|MAX]` and `ZINTERSTORE` write the result into `dest`.
- `ZUNION`, `ZINTER`, `ZDIFF` (6.2) return the result directly, and `ZINTERCARD` (7.0) returns only the size of the intersection.
- `ZRANGESTORE dest src min max [BYSCORE|BYLEX] [REV] [LIMIT ...]` (6.2) saves a slice of a sorted set into another key.

blocks.text: A game or a "bestsellers today" page needs three operations: record a result, show the top N, and show where one entry stands. They map to one command each.

blocks.code:
# a purchase of sku-42 happened: add one to its sales count
ZINCRBY lb:bestsellers:daily 1 sku-42
# top 10 products with their counts
ZRANGE lb:bestsellers:daily 0 9 REV WITHSCORES
# position of one product (0 = best)
ZREVRANK lb:bestsellers:daily sku-42
# a window "around me": 2 above and 2 below rank 14
ZRANGE lb:bestsellers:daily 12 16 REV WITHSCORES
# end of day: keep a copy, start fresh
RENAME lb:bestsellers:daily lb:bestsellers:2026-10-09

blocks.text:
All of these are O(log N) plus the size of the result. Hundreds of thousands of members are not a problem; tens of millions in one key are, because one key lives on one node and a huge `ZUNIONSTORE` will stall it. The later chapter on leaderboards in the Patterns Part covers sharding and pagination for that scale.

### Pattern: a time-ordered index

Use a Unix timestamp as the score and an ID as the member, and you have an index of "things by time" that supports range queries, which a list cannot do. `ZADD events:u42 1760000000 evt-9` adds, `ZRANGE events:u42 (1759990000` `+inf BYSCORE LIMIT 0 50` reads everything newer than a moment, and `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE events:u42 -inf` `1759000000` trims the old entries. The payloads live elsewhere, in hashes or strings keyed by the member ID; the sorted set is the ordered index.

### Pattern: a sliding-window rate limiter

Keep one sorted set per client. Each request is a member (made unique with a request ID) whose score is the timestamp in milliseconds. To check the limit, delete members older than the window, count what is left, and add the new request if there is room. Doing all this in one transaction or script keeps it atomic.

blocks.code:
# limit: 100 requests per 60 seconds, now = 1760000100000 ms
ZREMRANGEBYSCORE rl:1.2.3.4:/login 0 1760000040000
ZCARD rl:1.2.3.4:/login
# if the count is below 100:
ZADD rl:1.2.3.4:/login 1760000100000 req-7f3a
PEXPIRE rl:1.2.3.4:/login 60000

blocks.text:
This "sliding window log" is exact but stores one member per request, so memory grows with the limit. The rate-limiting chapter in the Patterns Part compares it with cheaper counters and token buckets and gives the Lua version that makes the steps atomic.

### Pattern: a delay queue

A job that must run at a future time goes into a sorted set with its due time as the score. Workers poll for jobs whose score is at or below the current time.

blocks.code:
# schedule: send reminder in 10 minutes (due = now + 600000 ms)
ZADD delayed:jobs 1760000700000 job:remind:1001
# worker: fetch one due job
ZRANGE delayed:jobs -inf 1760000100000 BYSCORE LIMIT 0 1
# claim it; only the worker whose ZREM returns 1 owns the job
ZREM delayed:jobs job:remind:1001

blocks.text:
The claim step matters: two workers may read the same member, but `ZREM` returns `1` for exactly one of them. The chapter on delayed and scheduled tasks turns this into a robust loop with a Lua script and a retry path.

### How sorted sets are stored

A small sorted set (up to `zset-max-listpack-entries`, default 128, with members no longer than `zset-max-listpack-value`, default 64 bytes) is a **listpack** of member and score pairs kept in order. Larger ones use a **skiplist** together with a **hashtable**. The skiplist is a layered linked list that gives O(log N) insertion, deletion and range access with simpler code than a balanced tree; the hashtable maps member to score so `ZSCORE` is O(1). Each member is stored once and referenced from both structures. The cost is a pointer-rich entry per member on top of the member itself, so a large sorted set is one of the heavier structures (measure with `MEMORY USAGE`); Redis 8.6 brought a memory reduction for skiplist-encoded sorted sets.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: A sorted set key grows forever unless you trim it. The time-ordered index, the log-style rate limiter and the leaderboard history all need an explicit `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE` or `ZREMRANGEBYRANK`, or a TTL on the whole key, as part of the same code path that adds members. Otherwise the key becomes a slow memory leak and, eventually, a very big key.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How would you build a real-time leaderboard for ten million players, and what are the limits? One sorted set with the player ID as the member and the score as the score. `ZINCRBY` or `ZADD GT` to record, `ZRANGE key 0 99 REV WITHSCORES` for the top 100, `ZREVRANK` for a player's position, and a window with `ZRANGE ... REV` around that rank. Every operation is O(log N). At ten million members the set holds a few GB and sits on one node, so a hot key concentrates load; split by region or season, or keep the top N only. Mention tie-breaking and that rank queries stay cheap while bulk `ZUNIONSTORE` does not.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A sorted set is unique members ordered by a floating-point score; ties break lexicographically by member.
- Updating a score replies `0` for `ZADD` unless you use `CH`; use `GT` for "best score wins" and `ZINCRBY` for counters.
- `ZRANGE` with `REV`, `BYSCORE`, `BYLEX` and `LIMIT` is the single read command; `ZRANK`, `ZREVRANK`, `ZPOPMIN` are O(log N).
- Typical uses: leaderboards, time-ordered indexes, sliding-window limiters, delay queues, priority queues.
- Storage is a listpack when small, otherwise a skiplist plus a hashtable; trim every sorted set that can grow.

The most useful skill when designing with Redis is picking the structure whose operations match your questions. Start from what you need to do, not from the data. Ask: do I read the whole value or part of it? Do I need order, uniqueness, ranges, counting, expiry per item? How big can it grow, and who writes concurrently?

### From need to structure

rows: Cache a value or a serialized object under a key
Store a record and update single fields
Rank by score, top-N, range by score or time
Delay queue, sliding window, priority queue
Count unique items approximately, in tiny memory
Yes/no flag per integer ID, huge ranges
Nested documents with partial updates, indexing

blocks.text:
Streams, HyperLogLog, bitmaps, geo, JSON and the search structures are covered in the next chapters of this Part.

### Worked examples

#### Shopping cart

Per-user carts with line quantities: a hash `cart:u42` with the SKU as field and the quantity as value. `HINCRBY cart:u42` `sku-1 1` adds one, `HDEL` removes a line, `HGETALL` renders it (carts are small). Set a key TTL (`EXPIRE cart:u42 604800`) so abandoned carts disappear. A list would make "change the quantity of sku-1" an O(N) search; a JSON string would force a read-modify-write.

#### Online users

A set `online` is simplest, but a crash leaves ghosts. A sorted set `online:zset` with the last-seen timestamp as the score fixes that: `ZADD online:zset <now> u42` on every heartbeat, `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE online:zset -inf <now - 60000>` to evict the silent, `ZCARD` to count.

#### "Customers also viewed"

For each product keep a sorted set `also:product:42` where the member is another product and the score the number of co-views: `ZINCRBY`. The top five is `ZRANGE also:product:42 0 4 REV`. A set would only say that two products were viewed together, not how often.

#### Unique visitors

A set gives exact counts and costs memory in proportion to the number of visitors. When millions of visitors per day only need an approximate number, a HyperLogLog is about 12 KB regardless of size. Decide whether you need the members back (set) or only the count (HyperLogLog).

### Mistakes to avoid

- Using a **list** as a database table and searching it with `LPOS`. Use a hash or sorted set.
- Packing a whole object into one **string** and then updating one field from many clients.
- Using a **set** where you need order or expiry per member; use a sorted set.
- Using a **sorted set** where a list is enough (a plain FIFO queue): you pay O(log N) and extra memory for ordering you do not need.
- One enormous key (a hash with ten million fields, a list that never drains). Split by a natural boundary.
- Forgetting that every key and structure needs a lifetime plan: a TTL, a trim, or a scheduled cleanup.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Choose by the question you must answer: lookup by key, order, uniqueness, range, counting, or hand-off.
- Strings for values and counters, hashes for records, lists for queues at the ends, sets for membership, sorted sets for anything ranked or time-ordered.
- Prefer many medium keys over a few giant ones; give each key a TTL or a trim rule.
- If two structures can do the job, pick the one with the cheaper operations for your hottest query.

ShopStream emits an event every time something happens to an order: created, paid, packed, shipped. Several services care about those events. The notification service sends e-mails, the inventory service adjusts stock, the analytics job counts revenue. You need a place to put the events so that each service can read them at its own pace, none of them loses an event when it restarts, and a slow reader does not hold up a fast one.

A list can act as a queue, but one consumer pops an item and it is gone. Pub/Sub can fan out to many readers, but it keeps nothing: a subscriber that is down misses the message forever (the next chapter shows this). What you want is a **log**: an append-only sequence of entries that stays in Redis, that readers walk through at their own position, and that can be shared out among a team of workers. That is the Redis **stream**, introduced in Redis 5.0 and extended in nearly every release since.

### The core idea: an append-only log with IDs

A stream is a key whose value is an ordered sequence of **entries**. Each entry has a unique **ID** and a set of field-value pairs, much like a small hash. You only ever append to the end (and trim from the front); entries are not updated in place.

blocks.code:
stream:orders
  ID                  fields
  1760000000000-0     orderId=1001  userId=7  total=59.90
  1760000000000-1     orderId=1002  userId=9  total=12.00
  1760000000500-0     orderId=1003  userId=7  total=5.25      ← newest, appended at the tail

blocks.text:
The ID has two parts, `<milliseconds>-<sequence>`. When you let Redis generate it (by passing `*`), the first part is the server time in milliseconds and the second part is a counter that distinguishes entries created in the same millisecond. IDs always increase, so the stream is automatically ordered by time of insertion, and you can ask for "everything since this ID" cheaply. Internally a stream is a radix tree of listpacks (compact blocks of entries), which gives O(1) append and fast lookup by ID.

#### Adding entries with XADD

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> XADD stream:orders * orderId 1001 userId 7 total 59.90
"1760000000000-0"
127.0.0.1:6379> XADD stream:orders * orderId 1002 userId 9 total 12.00
"1760000000000-1"
127.0.0.1:6379> XLEN stream:orders
(integer) 2
blocks.title: Append and measure

blocks.text:
`XADD key id field value [field value ...]` returns the ID it assigned. You may supply the ID yourself, but it must be greater than the last one or you get an error (`ERR The ID specified in XADD is equal or smaller than the` `target stream top item`). A partial ID such as `5-*` fixes the millisecond part and lets Redis choose the sequence. Explicit IDs are useful when importing data or in tests; production code almost always passes `*`.

`XADD` is O(1) when it only appends. Adding `NOMKSTREAM` prevents the command from creating the stream if the key does not exist.

#### Reading by range: XRANGE and XREVRANGE

`XRANGE key start end [COUNT n]` returns entries between two IDs, inclusive. The special IDs `-` and `+` mean "the smallest possible" and "the largest possible". A millisecond-only bound such as `1760000000000` matches every sequence number in that millisecond.

A `(` in front of an ID makes the bound **exclusive**. That is how you page through a stream: remember the last ID you processed and ask for `(lastId +`. `XREVRANGE key end start` walks backwards, which is the easy way to fetch the latest N entries (`XREVRANGE stream:orders + - COUNT 10`).

### Reading as a stream: XREAD

`XRANGE` is a query. To **follow** a stream, like `tail -f`, use `XREAD`, which takes one or more keys and, for each, the last ID you have seen. It returns entries with greater IDs.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> XREAD COUNT 2 STREAMS stream:orders 1760000000000-1
1) 1) "stream:orders"
   2) 1) 1) "1760000000500-0"
         2) 1) "orderId"
            2) "1003"
            3) "userId"
            4) "7"
            5) "total"
            6) "5.25"
127.0.0.1:6379> XREAD BLOCK 5000 STREAMS stream:orders $
(nil)
blocks.title: Follow a stream, with blocking

blocks.text:
Two details matter. First, `BLOCK 5000` makes the command wait up to 5000 ms for new data instead of returning immediately with an empty result; `BLOCK 0` waits forever. A blocked client costs almost nothing, so many consumers can wait on one stream. Second, the special ID `$` means "only entries added after this command starts". Use `$` for the first call, then switch to the real last-seen ID for every call after that. A classic bug is to pass `$` on every loop iteration, which silently skips every entry that arrived between two calls.

Plain `XREAD` has no memory: every reader keeps its own cursor and every reader sees every entry. For fan-out of the full stream to independent readers (an audit logger, a cache warmer), that is exactly right. For sharing work among a team it is not, and that is what consumer groups are for.

### Consumer groups: sharing the work

A **consumer group** is a named cursor on a stream, plus bookkeeping, shared by a set of **consumers**. The group remembers the ID of the last entry it handed out. Each new entry is delivered to exactly one consumer in the group, so adding consumers scales processing out. Different groups on the same stream are independent: the `notifier` group and the `inventory` group each see every order.

blocks.text:
#### The delivery cycle

1. Create the group once with `XGROUP CREATE key group id [MKSTREAM]`. The ID says where the group starts: `0` means "from the beginning of the stream", `$` means "only new entries". `MKSTREAM` creates the stream if it does not exist yet.
2. Each worker calls `XREADGROUP GROUP group consumer ... STREAMS key >`. The special ID `>` means "entries never delivered to any consumer in this group". Consumers do not need to be registered in advance; the first call creates them.
3. Redis records every delivered entry in the group's **Pending Entries List (PEL)**, with the consumer name, the delivery time and a delivery counter.
4. When the worker has finished the job it calls `XACK key group id [id ...]`, which removes the entries from the PEL.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> XGROUP CREATE stream:orders notifier 0
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> XREADGROUP GROUP notifier worker-1 COUNT 2 STREAMS stream:orders >
1) 1) "stream:orders"
   2) 1) 1) "1760000000000-0"
         2) 1) "orderId"
            2) "1001"
            3) "userId"
            4) "7"
            5) "total"
            6) "59.90"
      2) 1) "1760000000000-1"
         2) 1) "orderId"
            2) "1002"
            3) "userId"
            4) "9"
            5) "total"
            6) "12.00"
127.0.0.1:6379> XPENDING stream:orders notifier
1) (integer) 2
2) "1760000000000-0"
3) "1760000000000-1"
4) 1) 1) "worker-1"
      2) "2"
127.0.0.1:6379> XACK stream:orders notifier 1760000000000-0
(integer) 1
blocks.title: Create a group, read, inspect, acknowledge

blocks.text: The summary form of `XPENDING` shows how many entries are pending, the smallest and largest pending IDs, and how many each consumer holds. The extended form `XPENDING key group [IDLE min-idle-ms] start end count` `[consumer]` lists individual entries: ID, consumer, milliseconds since the last delivery, and the number of times it has been delivered.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> XPENDING stream:orders notifier - + 10
1) 1) "1760000000000-1"
   2) "worker-1"
   3) (integer) 184233
   4) (integer) 1
blocks.title: Pending entries in detail

blocks.text:
Read that as: entry `...-1` was given to `worker-1` 184 seconds ago and has been delivered once. If worker-1 crashed, this entry will sit there forever unless someone takes it over.

### At-least-once delivery and recovery

The PEL is what turns a stream into a reliable queue. A message is only forgotten when a worker explicitly acknowledges it. If the worker dies before acknowledging, the entry stays pending and can be handed to another worker. This gives **at-least-once** delivery: every entry is processed at least once, and sometimes twice (a worker may finish the work and crash before sending `XACK`). Your handler must therefore be idempotent, a topic the patterns part of the book returns to.

#### Taking over abandoned entries

`XAUTOCLAIM key group consumer min-idle-time start [COUNT n]` scans the PEL starting at `start`, transfers every entry that has been idle at least `min-idle-time` ms to `consumer`, and returns them with a cursor for the next call. It replaces the older two-step recipe of `XPENDING` followed by `XCLAIM` for most uses.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> XAUTOCLAIM stream:orders notifier worker-2 60000 0-0 COUNT 10
1) "0-0"
2) 1) 1) "1760000000000-1"
      2) 1) "orderId"
         2) "1002"
         3) "userId"
         4) "9"
         5) "total"
         6) "12.00"
3) (empty array)
blocks.title: Claim entries idle for more than 60 seconds

blocks.text:
The first element is the cursor to pass as `start` on the next call; `0-0` means the scan reached the end of the PEL. The last element lists IDs that were in the PEL but no longer exist in the stream (trimmed or deleted); Redis removes those dangling references for you. Claiming resets the idle timer and increments the delivery counter, so an entry that keeps crashing workers shows an ever-growing counter.

#### Claiming while reading (Redis 8.4)

Redis 8.4 added `CLAIM min-idle-time` to `XREADGROUP`. With it, a single call first returns pending entries that have been idle at least that long (longest idle first), then fills the rest with new entries when you read with `>`. Claimed entries carry two extra values: the milliseconds since last delivery and the delivery count. This lets one worker loop do both jobs:

blocks.code: XREADGROUP GROUP notifier worker-2 COUNT 10 BLOCK 2000 CLAIM 60000 STREAMS stream:orders >

blocks.text:
The reply layout for claimed entries is slightly different from a normal reply, so verify it against your client library before parsing it by hand. On servers older than 8.4 use `XAUTOCLAIM` in a periodic housekeeping task instead.

#### Re-reading your own pending entries

If a worker restarts it should first look at what it already owns. `XREADGROUP ... STREAMS stream:orders 0` (an ID instead of `>`) returns that consumer's own pending entries rather than new ones. A typical worker loop reads with `0` until the reply is empty, then switches to `>`.

#### Poison messages and dead letters

Some entries can never succeed: malformed payloads, a bug that throws every time. The delivery counter in `XPENDING` tells you how many attempts an entry has had. Redis has no built-in dead-letter queue, so the usual pattern is: when the counter passes a limit (say 5), the worker copies the entry to a second stream such as `stream:orders:dead` with `XADD`, then acknowledges the original. A human or a repair job looks at the dead stream later.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Never skip the acknowledgement path A worker that reads with `XREADGROUP` and never calls `XACK` makes the PEL grow without bound, and the stream cannot be trimmed safely. Acknowledge after the work is done (not before), and alert on `XPENDING` counts and on the oldest pending idle time.

### Keeping a stream from growing forever

A stream keeps its entries until you remove them. Reading, even acknowledging, does not delete anything: acknowledgement only affects the group's PEL. Left alone, a busy stream eats all your memory. There are three tools.

rows: Keep roughly the newest N entries
Drop entries with IDs older than id
Trim on a schedule instead of on every add
blocks.caption: Ways to bound a stream.

blocks.text: The `~` in `MAXLEN ~ 1000` asks for **approximate** trimming. Redis stores entries in macro nodes and only removes whole nodes, so the stream may keep slightly more than 1000 entries but trimming is far cheaper. Exact trimming (`=`, the default) can cut inside a node and costs more. For retention by time, compute the cutoff yourself, since an ID starts with milliseconds: to keep 7 days, pass `MINID ~ <nowMillis minus 604800000>`.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Trimming does not know about your consumers Plain `MAXLEN` and `MINID` remove entries even when a consumer group has not read them yet or still has them pending. A slow group then finds its entries gone, and `XAUTOCLAIM` reports them as deleted. Size the cap with the slowest consumer in mind, or use the group-aware options below.

#### Group-aware deletion (Redis 8.2)

Redis 8.2 added three ways to decide what happens to consumer group references when entries are deleted or trimmed. `XADD` and `XTRIM` accept an optional `KEEPREF | DELREF | ACKED` flag (default `KEEPREF`), and two new commands require one:

- `XDELEX key [KEEPREF | DELREF | ACKED] IDS numids id [id ...]` deletes entries.
- `XACKDEL key group [KEEPREF | DELREF | ACKED] IDS numids id [id ...]` acknowledges in the given group and deletes in one atomic step.

The three policies mean:

- **KEEPREF** (default): delete the entry but leave existing references in every group's PEL, like plain `XDEL`.
- **DELREF**: delete the entry and also remove its references from all PELs.
- **ACKED**: delete only entries that every consumer group has read and acknowledged. Entries still pending in some group stay.

Both commands reply with one integer per ID: `1` deleted, `-1` no such entry, `2` not deleted because references still exist (`ACKED` only).

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> XACKDEL stream:orders notifier ACKED IDS 1 1760000000000-1
1) (integer) 2
blocks.title: Acknowledge and delete only when all groups are done

blocks.text:
With two groups, the `notifier` group acknowledges the entry, but the `inventory` group has not, so the reply is `2`: acknowledged, not deleted. When `inventory` later runs the same command, the entry is gone. If you use several groups on one stream, `XACKDEL ... ACKED` replaces the error-prone pair `XACK` plus `XDEL`.

### Monitoring a stream with XINFO

`XINFO STREAM key` reports the length, first and last entries, the last generated ID and group count. `XINFO GROUPS key` shows each group's state and `XINFO CONSUMERS key group` shows each consumer.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> XINFO GROUPS stream:orders
1)  1) "name"
    2) "notifier"
    3) "consumers"
    4) (integer) 2
    5) "pending"
    6) (integer) 1
    7) "last-delivered-id"
    8) "1760000000000-1"
    9) "entries-read"
   10) (integer) 2
   11) "lag"
   12) (integer) 1
blocks.title: Group health at a glance

blocks.text:
`pending` is the size of the PEL; `lag` is how many entries the group has not been delivered yet. Together they say "how far behind is this group" and "is anything stuck". `XINFO CONSUMERS` adds an `idle` time per consumer, useful for noticing dead workers.

### Idempotent producers (Redis 8.6)

Producers also fail: a client sends `XADD`, the network drops before the reply arrives, and the client retries. Without protection the event appears twice. Redis 8.6 added producer-side deduplication to `XADD`:

blocks.code:
XADD stream:orders IDMP order-service ord-1001-created * orderId 1001 total 59.90
XADD stream:orders IDMPAUTO order-service * orderId 1001 total 59.90
XCFGSET stream:orders IDMP-DURATION 300 IDMP-MAXSIZE 1000

blocks.text:
`IDMP producer-id idempotent-id` tells Redis that this producer has a unique key for this message. If the same pair was used recently, `XADD` adds nothing and returns the ID of the original entry. `IDMPAUTO producer-id` lets Redis derive the idempotent ID from the content. Both work only with an auto-generated entry ID (`*`). `XCFGSET` sets how long (`IDMP-DURATION`, seconds) and how many (`IDMP-MAXSIZE`) idempotent IDs the stream remembers per producer. The window is bounded, so this protects against retries, not against duplicates hours apart.

### Streams, lists and Kafka

rows: Kept by time or size policy
Work sharing in a Yes group
Acknowledge and Manual with a second list retry
blocks.caption: Choosing a messaging structure.

blocks.text: Streams sit between a simple list and a full log platform. They are an excellent fit when the volume fits in memory, retention is hours or days, and you already run Redis. They are not a substitute for Kafka when you need terabytes of retained history, strict ordering across many partitions, or a large ecosystem of connectors. One more caveat: persistence and replication follow the usual Redis rules, so with default settings a crash can lose the most recent entries (see the persistence chapters).

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: ShopStream's order events `order-service` appends to `stream:orders` with `MAXLEN ~ 100000`. The `notification-service` runs three worker instances in group `notifier`; `inventory-service` has its own group. A scheduled task in each service calls `XAUTOCLAIM` every 30 seconds with a 60-second idle limit, and moves entries delivered more than five times to `stream:orders:dead`.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How do Redis Streams give at-least-once delivery, and what happens when a consumer crashes? A group's PEL records every entry delivered to a consumer until it calls `XACK`. If the consumer crashes, its entries stay pending. Another consumer takes them over with `XAUTOCLAIM` (or `XCLAIM`, or `XREADGROUP ... CLAIM` on 8.4+) after a minimum idle time, and the delivery counter increases. Because a crash after the work but before the `XACK` causes reprocessing, handlers must be idempotent.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between a Redis stream and Pub/Sub? Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget: messages are pushed to whoever is connected at that moment and are not stored. A stream stores entries, supports replay by ID, remembers each group's position and tracks acknowledgements.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A stream is an append-only log of entries with increasing IDs of the form `ms-seq`; append with `XADD`, read ranges with `XRANGE`, follow with `XREAD BLOCK`.
- A consumer group shares entries among workers; every delivered entry sits in the PEL until `XACK`, which gives at-least-once delivery.
- Recover from dead workers with `XAUTOCLAIM`; watch `XPENDING`, `XINFO GROUPS` lag and delivery counts, and send poison messages to a dead-letter stream yourself.
- Streams grow until you trim them: use `MAXLEN ~` or `MINID ~`, and on 8.2+ `XACKDEL ... ACKED` when several groups share a stream.
- Redis 8.6 adds `IDMP` and `IDMPAUTO` on `XADD` so producer retries do not create duplicates.

Sometimes you do not need a log. You need to tell whoever is listening right now that something happened: a cache entry changed, a chat message was typed, a configuration flag flipped. **Publish/subscribe** (Pub/Sub) is Redis's lightweight broadcast mechanism for exactly that. Senders publish a message to a named **channel**; every client currently subscribed to that channel receives a copy. The sender and receivers never know about each other.
